You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The test failure and issue report describe that the LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer ignores the VectorialConvergenceChecker parameter passed to it, which prevents customization of stopping criteria during optimization.

Looking at the constructor code snippet we could retrieve for LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer, we only see the default constructor:
```java
public LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer() {
    // set up the superclass with a default  max cost evaluations setting
    setMaxIterations(1000);

    // default values for the tuning parameters
    setInitialStepBoundFactor(100.0);
    setCostRelativeTolerance(1.0e-10);
    setParRelativeTolerance(1.0e-10);
    setOrthoTolerance(1.0e-10);
}
```
This default constructor does not show any handling or storing of a VectorialConvergenceChecker argument.

Our attempts to locate a constructor receiving a VectorialConvergenceChecker parameter failed to identify any code that stores or uses such a parameter.

From this, we can infer the following:
- The LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer class either does not have a constructor accepting a VectorialConvergenceChecker parameter OR such constructor does not use the parameter.
- Therefore, when the user attempts to pass a VectorialConvergenceChecker to customize stopping criteria, it is ignored.
- The optimizer likely uses some internal default convergence checker with no option to replace it.
- This behavior matches the bug report's statement that the VectorialConvergenceChecker parameter is ignored.

This explains why the test involving Minpack and the JennrichSampson function fails or behaves unexpectedly when substituting the VectorialConvergenceChecker — the parameter is not respected internally by the optimizer.

No use or invocation of the VectorialConvergenceChecker parameter was shown in the constructor or related visible code, suggesting a missing field assignment and no integration in the optimization logic.

Recent bug reports are unrelated and do not provide further insight into this problem.

The root cause is the lack of support for the VectorialConvergenceChecker parameter in LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer, specifically the absence of storing and using it.

This leads to ignoring the parameter, causing the test failure related to convergence checking.

Hence, the bug occurs because the LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer constructor does not handle the VectorialConvergenceChecker parameter, and the optimizer does not use any custom convergence checker given by callers.

This should be fixed by adding:
- a field to store the VectorialConvergenceChecker,
- acceptance of this parameter in constructor(s),
- and using it during optimization to control convergence.

This diagnosis explains the observed failure and matches the bug report.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
